title: K2tog decrease
sourceNotes: k2tog is a standard decrease described throughout Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s, public domain) and Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870, public domain). sourceType: PUBLIC_DOMAIN.

glossaryTerms.definition: Knit two together: the right needle enters two stitches at once and knits them as one, producing a right-leaning decrease.

content.text: The secret of
k2tog

(knit two together) is that it is simply a knit stitch worked through two stitches at once, so the first stitch lies over the second and the column naturally leans to the right. It is the most direct of all knitting decreases: one action, no preparatory slipping, one stitch removed.
You need yarn and needles. A swatch of 20 or more stitches in a smooth, plied yarn shows the right-leaning column clearly.
Step by step
Insert the right needle into the next two stitches on the left needle at once, from left to right through the front legs of both stitches together.
Wrap the yarn around the right needle as for a standard knit stitch.
Draw the new loop through both stitches and slide both original stitches off the left needle together. Two stitches have become one, leaning to the right.
Where you'll see it
k2tog is the most frequently used decrease in knitting. It appears in hat crown shaping (where multiple k2tog rounds converge the stitches toward the top), in lace patterns paired with
yarn overs
to produce directional lace motifs, in raglan seam shaping, and in the
heel turn
as the right-side row decrease. Virtually every knitted object with any shaping uses k2tog at least once.
Common faults
Entering only one stitch. If the needle enters the first stitch only and then the yarn is wrapped, no decrease is made. Check that the needle tip passes through both stitches before wrapping.

Decrease column twisting. If the right needle enters through the back of both stitches rather than the front, the stitch will be twisted (a k2tog tbl rather than k2tog). Both front legs of both stitches should be in front of the left needle when the right needle enters.
Wrong lean compared to
ssk
. K2tog leans right; ssk leans left. If both decreases in a pattern appear to lean the same way, one of them is being worked incorrectly. Swatch both side by side to compare.
What to try next: use k2tog and ssk together in a simple lace pattern. A yarn-over-and-decrease chevron works well. It shows clearly how the lean of each decrease shapes the direction of the fabric.
